findings.claim: Harper imagines a communal “song” giving “more abundant life” to everyone as her answer to conflict
findings.problem: 'Songs for the People' is a GUIDE ONLY text in the source document: the complete list of quotable spans is 'songs for the people', 'more abundant life', 'hearts of men', 'bright and restful mansions'. The bare word 'song' in quotation marks is not on that list, so it is an unverified quotation attributed to the poem. ('more abundant life' is correctly quoted.)
findings.correction: Harper imagines communal “songs for the people” giving “more abundant life” to everyone as her answer to conflict

findings.claim: Integrates relevant context (Lamb's Poetry for Children; Bennett's Windrush-era Jamaica) with sustained analysis of language and structure.
findings.problem: Contradicts the stated assessment rules: the poetry section of J352/02 assesses AO1 and AO2 ONLY, so AO3 is not assessed and there are no context marks in this section. Rewarding 'integrated context' misdirects revision toward material that cannot earn credit here.
findings.correction: Sustained, perceptive analysis of language, form and structure in both poems, with precise textual references supporting a developed personal response (AO1 and AO2 only — no marks are available for context in the poetry section).

findings.claim: Compare how Lamb in 'Envy' and Bennett in 'Colonization in Reverse' present conflict between different groups or ways of seeing the world.
findings.problem: Presented under the tariff type '20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison', but the assessment rules state that part a) prints the named anthology poem and an UNSEEN poem thematically linked to it, and asks students to compare those two printed poems. A comparison of two anthology poems is not a task on this paper; practising it as the 20-mark comparison misrepresents the exam.
findings.correction: Compare how Lamb presents conflict in 'Envy' and how the poet of the unseen poem printed opposite presents conflict. In your answer you should consider: the ideas and attitudes in each poem; the tone and atmosphere in each poem; the effects of the language and structure used. (Use 'Colonization in Reverse' separately for part b) practice.)

findings.claim: Compare how Lamb in 'Envy' and Kaminsky in 'We Lived Happily during the War' present ideas about responsibility for conflict.
findings.problem: Same structural error: the 20-mark comparison task compares one named anthology poem with an unseen poem printed on the paper, not two anthology poems (assessment rules, 'The poetry question').
findings.correction: Compare how Lamb presents responsibility for conflict in 'Envy' and how the poet of the unseen poem printed opposite presents responsibility for conflict. In your answer you should consider: the ideas and attitudes in each poem; the tone and atmosphere in each poem; the effects of the language and structure used.

findings.claim: Mastering: Perceptive comparison of methods — ... Secure: Clear comparison with well-chosen quotations from both poems ... Developing: Some comparison ... Emerging: Simple comments on one or both poems with limited analysis.
findings.problem: These graded bands (used on all six practice questions) imitate OCR's level-of-response band descriptors, which the assessment rules expressly forbid reproducing, paraphrasing or imitating. No such four-band scheme with these names exists for J352/02.
findings.correction: What a strong answer does: compares the two poems point by point, analysing how language, form and structure create meaning in each, and supports a developed personal response with precise textual references. (Marks are awarded for AO1 and AO2 only; refer students to OCR's published mark scheme rather than an unofficial band scheme.)

findings.claim: If Envy is the poem printed for the first part of the question, look for an unseen poem that also treats jealousy, comparison or self-acceptance
findings.problem: Misleading about exam structure: students do not select the unseen poem. The assessment rules state that the paper prints the named anthology poem and an unseen poem thematically linked to it; there is no choice of unseen text.
findings.correction: If Envy is the anthology poem printed for the first part of the question, the unseen poem printed beside it will be linked to it thematically — read it for its treatment of jealousy, comparison or self-acceptance, and organise your comparison around ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure.

findings.claim: the comparison task rewards work that moves between both poems as you make each point
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking behaviour. The assessment rules state only that part a) asks students to compare the two printed poems and lists three bullet points to consider; they say nothing about integrated versus sequential comparison being rewarded.
findings.correction: Integrating the two poems point by point is usually easier to sustain than writing about each poem in turn, and helps you cover the three bullet points (ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, effects of language and structure).

findings.claim: since a quotation you cannot recall exactly will not earn credit for close analysis of language
findings.problem: Invented marking claim. The assessment rules say the exam is closed text and that AO1 requires textual references 'including quotations'; nothing states that an inexactly recalled quotation earns no credit. Precise reference is helpful, but the stated penalty is fabricated.
findings.correction: Because the exam is closed text, learn a few short quotations such as “blind and senseless tree” and “some pretty flower in their own mind” so that you can refer closely to Lamb's language from memory.

findings.claim: Compare how conflict shapes coming of age in Boat Stealing and Thirteen. You should compare the poets' ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: Misrepresents the J352/02 poetry question format. Per the stated assessment rules, part a) (20 marks) asks candidates to compare the TWO POEMS PRINTED ON THE PAPER — the named anthology poem and a thematically linked UNSEEN poem. No question on this paper asks students to compare two anthology poems with each other; part b) asks for detailed exploration of one other anthology poem, not a comparison. Practising an anthology-to-anthology comparison under this tariff trains the wrong task.
findings.correction: Compare how conflict shapes coming of age in Boat Stealing and in the unseen poem printed opposite, which describes a teenager's first encounter with adult judgement. You should compare the poets' ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure. (Use Thirteen instead for a part b) style task: 'Explore how Femi presents conflict and growing up in Thirteen.')

findings.claim: Compare how Boat Stealing and We Lived Happily during the War present the idea of personal responsibility for wrongdoing. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: Same format error: the 20-mark comparison part a) compares the named anthology poem with the printed unseen poem, according to the stated OCR J352/02 assessment rules. Pairing two anthology poems is not an exam task on this paper, and the mark-scheme note compounds this by requiring quotation from a second anthology poem in a closed-text comparison of printed poems.
findings.correction: Compare how Boat Stealing and the unseen poem printed opposite, in which a speaker admits to standing by while harm was done, present the idea of personal responsibility for wrongdoing. You should compare ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure. (Keep We Lived Happily during the War for a part b) task: 'Explore how Kaminsky presents personal responsibility in We Lived Happily during the War.')

findings.claim: ‘Vergissmeinnicht’ offers a further contrast: where Byron’s dead soldiers are anonymous and viewed from a distance, Keith Douglas’s soldier is given a name, a lover and a body described in close, uncomfortable detail.
findings.problem: Narrative detail of 'Vergissmeinnicht' is wrong. In the source text of the poem the dead soldier is never named; the name 'Steffi' belongs to the girl in the photograph found in the gunpit ('the dishonoured picture of his girl / who has put: Steffi. Vergissmeinnicht.'). A student writing that Douglas names his soldier would make a factual error in the exam.
findings.correction: ‘Vergissmeinnicht’ offers a further contrast: where Byron’s dead soldiers are anonymous and viewed from a distance, Keith Douglas’s soldier is given a named lover — the girl who wrote “Steffi. Vergissmeinnicht.” on his photograph — and a body described in close, uncomfortable detail.

findings.claim: {"q": "Which anthology poem contrasts Byron's anonymous soldiers with a named soldier's lover and body?", "a": "Vergissmeinnicht, by Keith Douglas."}
findings.problem: The wording 'a named soldier's lover' reproduces the error above: the soldier in 'Vergissmeinnicht' is unnamed, and it is his girl who is named (Steffi) in the poem's text.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which anthology poem contrasts Byron's anonymous soldiers with an unnamed soldier whose lover is named on his photograph?", "a": "Vergissmeinnicht, by Keith Douglas."}

findings.claim: Compare how conflict and power are presented in 'The Destruction of Sennacherib' and in 'Colonization in Reverse'. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: This misrepresents the OCR J352/02 comparison task. The stated assessment rules say part a) prints two poems — the named poem from the OCR Poetry Anthology and an unseen poem thematically linked to it — and asks students to compare those two printed poems. The board never sets a comparison between two anthology poems, so practising this format under the 20-mark comparison tariff trains the wrong task.
findings.correction: Compare how conflict and power are presented in 'The Destruction of Sennacherib' and in an unseen poem printed alongside it. [Mastering: Perceptive comparison of how Byron and the unseen poet present power and its collapse — analysing Byron's simile progression and anapaestic rhythm against the unseen poem's own language and structure. Secure: Clear comparison with relevant quotations and explained analysis of both poems' treatment of power. Developing: Some comparison with relevant references to language or structure in one or both poems. Emerging: Simple points about conflict or power with limited analysis.]

findings.claim: Compare how Byron in 'The Destruction of Sennacherib' and D'Aguiar in 'Papa-T' present the retelling of old stories of conflict. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: Same format error: under the stated assessment rules the 20-mark comparison is always between the printed anthology poem and the printed unseen poem, never between two anthology poems. A second anthology poem is used only in part b), where it is explored on its own (not printed, student's own choice).
findings.correction: Explore how D'Aguiar presents the retelling of old stories of conflict in 'Papa-T', and how this compares with Byron's biblical retelling in 'The Destruction of Sennacherib' if you choose it for the single-poem task. [Mastering: Perceptive exploration of D'Aguiar's memory of his grandfather's 'no-nonsense recitals' of an older war poem, analysing what the poet suggests about learning from inherited stories of conflict. Secure: Clear analysis with relevant quotation and explained effects. Developing: Some relevant comment with textual reference. Emerging: Simple comments with limited analysis.]

findings.claim: A precise four-word quotation, correctly placed and analysed, earns more credit than a vague half-remembered paraphrase of a whole stanza.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how the paper is credited. The stated assessment rules say only that AO1 requires use of textual references including quotations and that the poetry section assesses AO1 and AO2; OCR publishes no statement that shorter exact quotation 'earns more credit' than paraphrase. Claims about relative credit must not be invented.
findings.correction: For the second part, where you choose a poem from memory, keep two or three short, exact quotations ready: AO1 asks you to support your interpretations with textual references, including quotations, so accurate wording you can actually analyse is more useful to you than a half-remembered stanza.

findings.claim: {"q": "Which biblical city does the poem's story say the Assyrian army marched against?", "a": "Jerusalem, the city the Assyrian army besieged."}
findings.problem: Flashcard rule breach: the answer restates the question (the question already says the Assyrian army marched against the city). A bare one-word answer is acceptable here because the question begins 'Which'.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which biblical city does the poem's story say the Assyrian army marched against?", "a": "Jerusalem."}

findings.claim: The final line describes the army as “unsmote by the sword” yet “melted like snow” once a greater power turned against it.
findings.problem: Imprecise reference to the source text. Both phrases come from the poem's closing couplet, not a single final line, and they describe 'the might of the Gentile': 'And the might of the Gentile, unsmote by the sword, / Hath melted like snow in the glance of the Lord!'
findings.correction: The closing couplet describes “the might of the Gentile, unsmote by the sword” as having “melted like snow in the glance of the Lord” once a greater power turned against it.

findings.claim: This poem works well for the comparison task because its rhythm, imagery and biblical framing give you plenty to discuss under ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure.
findings.problem: Slightly misleading about the paper's structure: under the stated assessment rules the anthology poem used in part a) is named and printed by the paper, so students cannot select this poem for the comparison; their own choice applies only to part b). The three bullet areas quoted are correct.
findings.correction: If ‘The Destruction of Sennacherib’ is the anthology poem printed on your paper, its rhythm, imagery and biblical framing give you plenty to discuss under the three bullets you are given: ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure.

findings.claim: Compare how Harper presents the power of sound and music in 'Songs for the People' with how Byron presents the sound of war in 'The Destruction of Sennacherib'. You should compare the poets' use of language, form and structure. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: Misrepresents the exam task. The stated assessment rules for J352/02 say part a) prints the named anthology poem alongside an UNSEEN poem thematically linked to it, and asks students to compare those two printed poems; the paper never asks students to compare two anthology poems (the exam is closed text and the anthology may not be taken in). Practising an anthology-to-anthology comparison under this tariff trains the wrong task.
findings.correction: Compare how Harper presents the power of sound and music in 'Songs for the People' with how the poet of the unseen poem presents the sounds of war. You should compare the ideas and attitudes in each poem, the tone and atmosphere of each poem, and the effects of the language and structure used. [Byron's 'The Destruction of Sennacherib' should be set instead as a part b) single-poem exploration or as untimed comparison practice, not as a part a) task.]

findings.claim: Compare how Harper in 'Songs for the People' and Douglas in 'Vergissmeinnicht' present what survives after conflict. You should compare the poets' use of language, form and structure. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: Same structural error: the assessment rules state that the 20-mark comparison compares the named anthology poem with an unseen poem printed on the paper. A comparison of two anthology poems is not a question format that exists on this paper, and neither poem would be available in a closed-text exam.
findings.correction: Compare how Harper presents what survives conflict in 'Songs for the People' with how the poet of the unseen poem presents it. You should compare the ideas and attitudes in each poem, the tone and atmosphere of each poem, and the effects of the language and structure used. [Use 'Vergissmeinnicht' separately as a part b) single-poem exploration.]

findings.claim: The poem’s closing lines draw on softer, nurturing imagery, traditionally associated with the feminine, to complete this transformation, turning hardened “hearts of men” towards a gentler future. Harper pictures the destination of her music as “bright and restful mansions”
findings.problem: Wrong position in the poem. 'Bright and restful mansions' belongs to the stanza addressed to the poor and aged, not to the poem's ending; the poem's final lines are the ones about hearts of men grown tender girdling the world with peace (verified against Poetry Foundation / Poets.org / Harper's 1896 Poems, and consistent with OCR's own guide, whose question 10 places 'hearts of men' in the final lines).
findings.correction: The poem’s closing lines draw on softer, nurturing imagery, traditionally associated with the feminine, to complete this transformation, turning hardened “hearts of men” towards a gentler future of peace. Earlier, singing to the poor and aged, Harper pictures a place of comfort and permanence as “bright and restful mansions”

findings.claim: The repeated phrase “songs for the people” running through the poem reinforces this collective goal: the music belongs to everyone, not to one side of a conflict.
findings.problem: The exact wording 'songs for the people' occurs in the title and the opening line only; the repetition that runs through the poem is the anaphoric opening of each stanza, in which Harper repeatedly asks to make or sing songs for different groups (the weary, little children, the poor and aged). Verified against the poem text (Poetry Foundation, Poets.org, Harper's 1896 Poems); OCR's guide also locates the repetition in the stanza openings from the first stanza onwards.
findings.correction: The repeated stanza openings, in which Harper asks again and again to make or sing songs — for the people, for the weary, for little children, for the poor and aged — reinforce this collective goal: the music belongs to everyone, not to one side of a conflict.

findings.claim: For the single-poem task, the ballad stanza, the binary opposition between conflict and harmony, and the closing image of “bright and restful mansions” are all strong, quotable details
findings.problem: 'Bright and restful mansions' is not the closing image; it appears in the stanza sung for the poor and aged, and the poem closes on hearts of men grown tender and peace encircling the world (verified against the poem text on Poetry Foundation / Poets.org).
findings.correction: For the single-poem task, the ballad stanza, the binary opposition between conflict and harmony, and the image of “bright and restful mansions” offered to the poor and aged are all strong, quotable details

findings.claim: For the comparison task, Songs for the People works well against any poem that uses sound, music or rhythm to represent conflict or its absence
findings.problem: Implies students choose the pairing for the 20-mark comparison. Under the stated assessment rules the paper prints the named anthology poem and a thematically linked unseen poem, and students compare those two; the only free choice is the poem for part b), which must be a different anthology poem.
findings.correction: For the comparison task, the poems are set for you: if Songs for the People is the printed anthology poem, you compare it with the unseen poem printed beside it, so practise linking its sound and rhythm to whatever an unfamiliar poem does with sound and atmosphere

findings.claim: In the comparison task, examiners want to see language, form and structure discussed side by side, not two separate paragraphs bolted together.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner preference. The assessment rules state only that part a) asks students to compare the two printed poems and carries three bullet points (ideas and attitudes; tone and atmosphere; the effects of language and structure); nothing published states this about what examiners 'want'.
findings.correction: In the comparison task the question itself asks you to compare, and its bullet points direct you to the ideas and attitudes in each poem, the tone and atmosphere of each poem, and the effects of the language and structure used — so keep the two poems side by side rather than writing about each in turn.

findings.claim: {"q": "What image ends the poem representing peace and permanence?", "a": "'Bright and restful mansions.'"}
findings.problem: Factually wrong: the poem ends with hearts of men grown tender girdling the world with peace; 'bright and restful mansions' comes in the stanza sung for the poor and aged (verified against Poetry Foundation / Poets.org / Harper's 1896 Poems).
findings.correction: {"q": "Which image does Harper offer the poor and aged as a place of peace and permanence?", "a": "'Bright and restful mansions.'"}

findings.claim: {"q": "What phrase repeats through the poem to stress its collective goal?", "a": "'Songs for the people.'"}
findings.problem: The exact phrase appears only in the title and opening line; what recurs is the anaphoric stanza opening in which Harper asks to make or sing songs for successive groups. Verified against the poem text (Poetry Foundation, Poets.org).
findings.correction: {"q": "What kind of repetition opens Harper's stanzas and stresses her collective goal?", "a": "Anaphora: each stanza opens with the speaker asking to make or sing songs for another group."}

findings.claim: Mastering: Perceptive comparison of both poems' hopeful visions, analysing Harper's ballad stanza, repetition of 'songs for the people', and closing image of 'bright and restful mansions' against the unseen poem's chosen methods
findings.problem: Two textual errors in the guidance: 'songs for the people' is not repeated through the poem (it occurs in the title and first line; the repetition is the anaphoric stanza openings), and 'bright and restful mansions' is not the closing image (the poem closes on hearts of men grown tender and peace). Verified against the poem text on Poetry Foundation / Poets.org.
findings.correction: Mastering: Perceptive comparison of both poems' hopeful visions, analysing Harper's ballad stanza, the anaphoric stanza openings asking to make songs for successive groups, and the consoling image of 'bright and restful mansions' against the unseen poem's chosen methods, with real depth on tone and atmosphere.

findings.claim: exploring how repetition of 'songs for the people' structures its collective vision
findings.problem: Same error: the phrase itself is not repeated across the poem; the structuring repetition is the anaphora at the start of each stanza (asking to make or sing songs for the people, the weary, little children, the poor and aged). Verified against the poem text on Poetry Foundation / Poets.org.
findings.correction: exploring how the anaphoric stanza openings, in which Harper asks repeatedly to make or sing songs for a new group, structure its collective vision

findings.claim: Compare how Dickinson's 'There's a Certain Slant of Light' and John Agard's 'Flag' present power that feels impersonal and beyond individual control. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: This misrepresents the J352/02 poetry question as set out in the stated assessment rules. Part a) (20 marks) compares the named anthology poem with an UNSEEN poem printed alongside it on the paper; it never asks for a comparison of two anthology poems. A second anthology poem is used only in part b), which asks for a detailed exploration of ONE other anthology poem of the student's own choice, not printed and not compared. Practising an anthology-to-anthology comparison under the part a) tariff trains a task that cannot appear on this paper.
findings.correction: Compare how Dickinson in 'There's a Certain Slant of Light' and an unseen poem present power that feels impersonal and beyond individual control. You should compare the poets' ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of their language and structure. (If you wish to use Agard's 'Flag', set it as a separate '20 marks — Single Poem Exploration' task: 'Explore how Agard presents power that feels impersonal and beyond individual control in "Flag".')

findings.claim: Rather than full rhyme, Dickinson favours slant rhyme — pairs such as “scar” and “are” chime without matching exactly.
findings.problem: Wrong example. In the source text the stanza-two rhyme is 'scar' / 'are', which is an exact (full) rhyme in standard pronunciation, not a slant rhyme. Published analyses of this poem cite the genuine near-rhymes as 'Afternoons' / 'Tunes' in stanza one and 'breath' / 'Death' in the final stanza (e.g. Interesting Literature and Poem Analysis both single out the breath/Death rhyme). A student offering 'scar'/'are' as evidence of slant rhyme would be identifying the feature incorrectly under AO2.
findings.correction: Rather than full rhyme, Dickinson often favours slant rhyme — pairs such as “Afternoons” and “Tunes,” and the closing “breath” and “Death,” chime without matching exactly.

findings.claim: Mastering: Detailed exploration of the common metre borrowed from hymn tradition and the slant rhymes (such as 'scar' and 'are'), analysing how these formal choices echo religious certainty while the content undercuts it.
findings.problem: Same error as in the content: 'scar' / 'are' is a full rhyme, not a slant rhyme. The poem's slant rhymes are 'Afternoons' / 'Tunes' and 'breath' / 'Death'. Rewarding 'scar'/'are' as slant rhyme in a model answer would embed a technical mistake.
findings.correction: Mastering: Detailed exploration of the hymn-derived stanza form and the slant rhymes (such as 'breath' and 'Death'), analysing how these formal choices echo religious certainty while the content undercuts it.

findings.claim: Her frequent dashes interrupt each line, forcing pauses that mimic hesitation
findings.problem: Imprecise against the source text: most of Dickinson's dashes fall at line endings (e.g. 'Winter Afternoons –', 'Of Cathedral Tunes –'), and only some lines are interrupted mid-line ('None may teach it – Any –', 'Shadows – hold their breath –'). Not every line contains an interrupting dash.
findings.correction: Her frequent dashes break up the lines — closing most of them and cutting across others, as in “None may teach it – Any –” — forcing pauses that mimic hesitation

findings.claim: Because the comparison task weights analysis of language, form and structure slightly more heavily than ideas alone
findings.problem: The stated assessment rules say only that part a) places more weight on AO2 than on AO1; OCR publishes no per-question AO mark split and no statement of how large the difference is. The word 'slightly' quantifies a weighting the specification is silent about.
findings.correction: Because the comparison task places more weight on analysis of language, form and structure (AO2) than on ideas and personal response (AO1)

findings.claim: "Compare how Bennett in 'Colonization in Reverse' and Agard in 'Flag' present ideas about identity and loyalty." — type: "20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison"
findings.problem: This misrepresents the J352/02 poetry task. The stated assessment rules say part a) prints the named anthology poem alongside an UNSEEN poem thematically linked to it, and asks students to compare those two printed poems; a second anthology poem is never the comparison partner in part a). Part b) is a single-poem exploration of one other anthology poem, not a comparison. Practising an anthology-to-anthology comparison under this question type trains a task the paper does not set.
findings.correction: Compare how Bennett in 'Colonization in Reverse' and the poet of the unseen poem present ideas about identity and loyalty. (If retaining the 'Flag' pairing, relabel it as untimed comparison practice, not a '20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison' exam question.)

findings.claim: "Compare how Bennett in 'Colonization in Reverse' and D'Aguiar in 'Papa-T' present the West Indian relationship with an imagined 'motherland' or homeland." — type: "20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison"
findings.problem: Same structural error: per the stated assessment rules, the 20-mark comparison task compares the named anthology poem with the unseen poem printed on the paper, not with a second anthology poem. Labelling a two-anthology-poem comparison as the exam's comparison question teaches an exam format that does not exist on this component.
findings.correction: Compare how 'Colonization in Reverse' and an unseen poem present a speaker's relationship with an imagined 'motherland' or homeland. (Keep the 'Papa-T' link as comparison-thinking practice or as a part b) single-poem choice, not as a '20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison' question.)

findings.claim: a slightly wrong quotation from memory in the single-poem task will cost you marks that accurate paraphrase would not
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking behaviour. The stated assessment rules say the poetry section assesses AO1 and AO2 only, with AO1 requiring textual references including quotations; nothing in the specification states that a slightly misremembered quotation is penalised relative to paraphrase, and no SPaG/AO4 marks are available in this section. This is an invented examiner claim.
findings.correction: Learn the short quoted phrases in Jamaican Creole spelling so you can use precise textual detail from memory in the closed-book single-poem task; where you are unsure of exact wording, a close reference to the poem still supports your point.

findings.claim: matching the “calypso culture” of the 1950s Caribbean community she is celebrating
findings.problem: 'calypso culture' is placed in quotation marks twice (also in the Form and Structure section: "the rhythm and comic timing of the “calypso culture”"). It is OCR's teacher-guide commentary, not wording from the poem, and it is not on the permitted quotable-span list for this GUIDE ONLY poem ('tun history upside dung', 'de motherlan', 'motherlan', 'bag an baggage', 'loyalty', 'Miss Mattie'). Students could reproduce it in the exam as a quotation from Bennett.
findings.correction: matching the calypso culture of the 1950s Caribbean community she is celebrating (remove the quotation marks in both places, so the phrase reads as critical description rather than as a quotation from the poem)

findings.claim: Compare how conflict and its alternatives are presented in 'Vergissmeinnicht' and 'Songs for the People'. You should compare the poets' ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: This misrepresents the structure of the J352/02 poetry question as set out in the stated assessment rules: part a) (20 marks) asks students to compare the named anthology poem printed on the paper with an UNSEEN poem printed beside it — it never asks for a comparison of two anthology poems. Part b) (20 marks) is a single-poem exploration of one other anthology poem of the student's choice. Practising an anthology-to-anthology comparison as though it were the 20-mark comparison task trains a task that does not exist on this paper.
findings.correction: An unseen poem imagines a world in which music and song replace war. Compare how this unseen poem and 'Vergissmeinnicht' present conflict and its alternatives. You should compare the poets' ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]

findings.claim: The poem’s central idea is stated directly in its fifth stanza: ‘the lover and killer are mingled / who had one body and one heart’.
findings.problem: Wrong stanza location. In the source text these lines open the sixth and final quatrain ('For here the lover and killer are mingled / who had one body and one heart'); the fifth stanza is the one beginning 'But she would weep to see today'. The lesson elsewhere correctly states the poem has six quatrains, so this is internally inconsistent as well as wrong.
findings.correction: The poem’s central idea is stated directly in its final, sixth stanza: ‘the lover and killer are mingled / who had one body and one heart’.

findings.claim: For ‘Vergissmeinnicht’, a common mistake is describing the graphic imagery of decay without linking it back to the poem’s central idea — that the same body held both a lover and a killer. Always tie close language analysis back to that duality, and keep quotations short and exact: two or three words used precisely score higher than a half-remembered longer phrase.
findings.problem: Two unevidenced claims about candidate behaviour and marking. The stated assessment rules for J352/02 say only that the poetry section assesses AO1 and AO2 and publish no statement about frequent candidate errors or about quotation length affecting marks; nothing in OCR's published material states that shorter quotations score higher. Presenting this as exam-marking fact is a fabrication about examiner behaviour.
findings.correction: For ‘Vergissmeinnicht’, make sure any description of the graphic imagery of decay is linked back to the poem’s central idea — that the same body held both a lover and a killer. The poetry section rewards AO1 (informed personal response supported by textual reference) and AO2 (analysis of language, form and structure), so tie close language analysis back to that duality and use quotations you can reproduce accurately from memory, since the paper is closed text.

findings.claim: The single-word command ‘Look.’ interrupts the third stanza

findings.correction: {"q": "What single-word command opens the third stanza of the poem?", "a": "'Look.'"}

findings.claim: “What Were They Like?” is built from nine questions followed by answers
findings.problem: The source text of the poem contains six questions (lanterns of stone; ceremonies to reverence the opening of buds; quiet laughter; bone, ivory, jade and silver ornament; an epic poem; distinguishing speech from singing), each answered in turn. Published analyses of the poem also describe six numbered questions and six responses. 'Nine' is factually wrong and would be penalised as an inaccurate structural claim.
findings.correction: “What Were They Like?” is built from six questions followed by six answers

findings.claim: nine hopeful questions crowd the opening, while the answers that follow are calm, flat and devastating
findings.problem: The poem asks six questions, not nine (see source text lines 1-9, which form six interrogatives). Wrong structural count.
findings.correction: six hopeful questions crowd the opening, while the six answers that follow are calm, flat and devastating

findings.claim: After reading, explain why the poem's two halves — nine questions, then their answers — change pace from curiosity to horror.
findings.problem: The poem has six questions, not nine, according to the source text.
findings.correction: After reading, explain why the poem's two halves — six questions, then their answers — change pace from curiosity to horror.

findings.claim: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of how the poem's unbalanced structure — nine open questions against calm, devastating answers — controls the reader's shift from curiosity to horror.
findings.problem: The poem contains six questions, not nine (source text).
findings.correction: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of how the poem's unbalanced structure — six open questions against calm, devastating answers — controls the reader's shift from curiosity to horror.

findings.claim: When the questioner asks whether the Vietnamese people had “an epic poem,” the answer does not confirm or deny it; it simply reports that their speech, once like a song, has faded to an echo, because “It is silent now.”
findings.problem: Wrong question-answer pairing against the source text. The answer to the fifth question ('Had they an epic poem?') is 'It is not remembered. Remember, / most were peasants; their life / was in rice and bamboo.' The 'echo yet / of their speech which was like a song' is the answer to the sixth question, 'Did they distinguish between speech and singing?'
findings.correction: When the questioner asks whether the Vietnamese people had “an epic poem,” the answer refuses the question: “It is not remembered” is followed by the reminder that “most were peasants” whose life “was in rice and bamboo.” Only the final question, about speech and singing, receives the answer that their speech survives as “an echo yet” before “It is silent now.”

findings.claim: Match each question from the poem to the answer that negates it: 'Had they an epic poem?' → 'Their speech, once like a song, survives only as an echo.'
findings.problem: Mis-pairs question and answer against the source text. 'Had they an epic poem?' is answered by 'It is not remembered. Remember, / most were peasants; their life / was in rice and bamboo.' The echo of speech 'like a song' answers the separate question 'Did they distinguish between speech and singing?'
findings.correction: Match each question from the poem to the answer that negates it: left = ['Did they use lanterns of stone?', 'Were they inclined to quiet laughter?', 'Had they an epic poem?']; right = ['It is not remembered whether stone lanterns lit peaceful gardens.', 'Laughter is bitter to the burned mouth.', 'It is not remembered — most were peasants, whose life was in rice and bamboo.']

findings.claim: Constant enjambment — for example, the line break inside “their speech which was like a song” — keeps images incomplete until the next line resolves them
findings.problem: There is no line break inside that phrase in the source text. The lines read 'There is an echo yet / of their speech which was like a song.' The enjambment falls after 'yet', not within the quoted phrase, so the illustrative example does not exist as described.
findings.correction: Constant enjambment — for example, “There is an echo yet / of their speech which was like a song” — keeps images incomplete until the next line resolves them

findings.claim: The phrase “It is not remembered” recurs twice, almost word for word — an example of anaphora.
findings.problem: Terminology misapplied against the lesson's own glossary definition (repetition at the start of SUCCESSIVE clauses or lines). In the source text the two occurrences are widely separated (answer 1 and answer 5), so this is simple repetition, not anaphora. The poem's actual anaphora is the run of 'Did they' openings in the questions.
findings.correction: The phrase “It is not remembered” recurs twice, word for word — a repeated refrain. (The poem's true anaphora is the run of questions beginning “Did they”.)

findings.claim: Q: 'What technique names the repetition of "It is not remembered" across the poem?' A: 'Anaphora — repetition at the start of successive clauses.'
findings.problem: Factually wrong use of the term: the two occurrences of 'It is not remembered' are not in successive clauses or lines (they fall in the first and fifth answers), so the card teaches a terminology error that would be marked down under AO2. The poem's anaphora is the repeated 'Did they' in the questions.
findings.correction: Q: 'Which repeated opening in the poem's questions is an example of anaphora?' A: 'The repeated "Did they" at the start of the questions; "It is not remembered" is a separated refrain, not anaphora.'

findings.claim: a misquoted “It is not remembered” loses accuracy marks that a well-chosen short phrase would otherwise earn
findings.problem: Invented marking claim. <assessment_rules> states the poetry section assesses AO1 and AO2 only, with no marks for spelling and punctuation and no separate 'accuracy marks'. OCR publishes no such deduction for a misquotation.
findings.correction: make sure your quotations are exact — short, precisely remembered phrases support your points more convincingly than half-remembered longer ones, and the exam is closed text so you cannot check the anthology

findings.claim: several answers begin with the single word “Sir”
findings.problem: In the source text only two answers begin with 'Sir' ('Sir, their light hearts turned to stone.' and 'Sir, laughter is bitter to the burned mouth.'). 'Several' overstates the frequency.
findings.correction: two of the answers begin with the single word “Sir”

findings.claim: Levertov did not report from Vietnam; instead, she imagined a conversation
findings.problem: Stated too absolutely: Levertov had not visited Vietnam when she wrote this poem in the mid-1960s, but she did travel to Hanoi with Muriel Rukeyser in 1972 and wrote about what she saw there (recorded in 'The Poet in the World' and 'The Freeing of the Dust').
findings.correction: Levertov had not yet been to Vietnam when she wrote this poem (she visited Hanoi in 1972); here she imagines a conversation

findings.claim: The alliteration of the “scalded ocean and the blazing well” hammers together the destruction of water and land through the oil fires.
findings.problem: There is no alliteration in this phrase — no repeated initial consonant sounds ('scalded ocean and the blazing well'). Verified against the source text of 'Lament' (Poem 9, full text). Teaching an inaccurate terminology label risks students misapplying the term in an AO2 answer, where accurate subject terminology is credited.
findings.correction: The paired phrasing of the “scalded ocean and the blazing well” hammers together the destruction of water and land through the oil fires, the balanced grammar of the two halves making sea and earth share a single fate.

findings.claim: Byron’s ‘The Destruction of Sennacherib’ also shows military symbols — spears ‘gleaming in purple and gold’ — losing their power once the human cost becomes visible
findings.problem: Misattributes the image within the poem. The source text reads 'And his cohorts were gleaming in purple and gold'; it is the Assyrian host, not their spears, that gleams in purple and gold. The spears have a separate image: 'the sheen of their spears was like stars on the sea'. A student repeating this in an answer would be shown to have misread the line.
findings.correction: Byron’s ‘The Destruction of Sennacherib’ also shows military symbols — the Assyrian cohorts ‘gleaming in purple and gold’ and the ‘sheen of their spears’ — losing their power once the human cost becomes visible

findings.problem: In the source text 'purple and gold' describes the gleaming cohorts (the army itself), not armour specifically. The mark-scheme wording embeds the same misreading as the content section.
findings.correction: Perceptively compares Agard's ironic refrain 'It's just a piece of cloth' with Byron's glittering imagery of cohorts 'gleaming in purple and gold'

findings.claim: The near-rhymes at the end of each stanza — breeze/knees, pole/bold, tent/relent — give the poem a sing-song, almost nursery-rhyme quality
findings.problem: Two of the three pairs cited are full rhymes, not near-rhymes: breeze/knees and tent/relent rhyme exactly in the source text; only pole/bold (and field/bleed in stanza four) are half-rhymes. Labelling full rhymes as near-rhyme is a terminology slip in an AO2 point about sound.
findings.correction: Each tercet rhymes its first and last lines — full rhymes in breeze/knees and tent/relent, half-rhymes in pole/bold and field/bleed — giving the poem a sing-song, almost nursery-rhyme quality

findings.claim: What rhyme device creates the poem's unsettling sing-song tone? / "Near-rhyme, such as breeze and knees."

findings.correction: {"q": "What rhyme device creates the poem's unsettling sing-song tone?", "a": "Rhyme between the first and last line of each tercet, including half-rhymes such as pole and bold."}

findings.claim: Tennyson’s cavalrymen simply “do and die”, following orders without question.
findings.problem: The source text's quotable-spans note for 'Papa-T' states that Tennyson must never be quoted in this lesson; 'do and die' is licensed only as it appears within D'Aguiar's poem, not as a quotation from 'The Charge of the Light Brigade'. The lesson's own exam tip also tells students never to quote Tennyson, so the attribution is self-contradictory.
findings.correction: D’Aguiar’s poem recalls Tennyson’s cavalrymen as men who simply “do and die”, following orders without question.

findings.claim: {"q": "According to Tennyson's poem, what do the soldiers simply do when given orders?", "a": "They 'do and die'."}
findings.problem: The card presents 'do and die' as a quotation from Tennyson's poem. The source text forbids quoting Tennyson in this lesson; the phrase is licensed only as wording inside D'Aguiar's 'Papa-T'.
findings.correction: {"q": "How does 'Papa-T' describe the obedience of Tennyson's soldiers?", "a": "As men who simply 'do and die' when given orders."}

findings.claim: For “Papa-T”, a common mistake is describing Tennyson’s poem as if it were an anthology poem
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how candidates typically perform; the stated assessment rules and OCR's published materials make no such statement about common candidate errors.
findings.correction: For “Papa-T”, remember that Tennyson’s poem is not one of your anthology poems, so it should be referred to only as the poem D’Aguiar’s grandfather recites

findings.claim: The title becomes the poem’s first line, so the confession begins before the poem has properly started — there is no gap between naming the poem and making the guilty admission.
findings.problem: Factually wrong about the poem's structure. In Kaminsky's text (Library of Congress Poetry 180; Poetry Out Loud; Deaf Republic, Graywolf) the poem's first line is 'And when they bombed other people's houses, we'. The title phrase is not the first line — it is echoed in the poem's FINAL sentence ('we (forgive us) / lived happily during the war'). OCR's own guide (Version 2 teacher guide, Q8) describes the opening as running on from the title into the poem, not the title being repeated as line one.
findings.correction: The poem opens abruptly in mid-thought, running on from its title straight into “they bombed other people’s houses”, and only returns to the title’s words in its closing lines — so the confession frames the whole poem, ending where the title began.

findings.claim: The speaker admits “We lived happily during the war,” then adds a parenthetical aside, “forgive us”, directly after it.
findings.problem: Misplaces the parenthesis. In the poem the aside comes at the very end and interrupts the phrase from within: 'our great country of money, we (forgive us) / lived happily during the war' (Library of Congress Poetry 180; Poetry Out Loud). It does not follow the opening admission. OCR's guide (Q10) treats the parenthesis as something that makes the reader re-read the title phrase, i.e. it arrives after the poem's list of 'money' lines, not at the start.
findings.correction: The poem’s closing sentence interrupts itself with a parenthetical aside: the speaker says “forgive us” in the middle of admitting that they “lived happily during the war”, so the plea for pardon is embedded inside the confession itself.

findings.claim: and the closing image of an “invisible house”, which suggests a safety that was never really solid
findings.problem: 'Invisible house' is not the closing image. It appears roughly mid-poem, immediately after the colon following 'America / was falling: invisible house by invisible house by invisible house' (Library of Congress Poetry 180; OCR guide Q7, which places it after that colon). The poem closes on 'lived happily during the war'.
findings.correction: and the repeated “invisible house” that follows the colon after “America was falling”, which suggests a safety that was never really solid

findings.claim: {"q": "What image closes the poem, suggesting a safety that was never solid?", "a": "An 'invisible house.'"}
findings.problem: Same error as above: 'invisible house' occurs mid-poem, directly after 'America / was falling:'; the poem's closing words are 'lived happily during the war'. A student answering this in the exam would misplace the image.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which repeated image follows the colon after 'America was falling', suggesting a safety that was never solid?", "a": "The 'invisible house', repeated three times."}

findings.claim: the phrase “of money” is repeated four times in a list, mimicking the small, selfish justifications — house, comfort, income — that kept the speaker looking inward instead of outward
findings.problem: The list is misdescribed. The fourfold repetition attaches to an outward-widening sequence of places — house of money, street of money, city of money, country of money (Library of Congress Poetry 180; Poetry Out Loud) — not to 'house, comfort, income'. The structure zooms out from the private home to the whole nation, implicating a national economy rather than personal comforts. OCR's guide (Q6) asks specifically about 'the structure of this list'.
findings.correction: the phrase “of money” is repeated four times in a widening list — house, street, city, country — so the frame pulls outwards from one home to a whole nation built on wealth, implicating far more than one household

findings.claim: while Kaminsky’s repeated “of money” lists smaller domestic comforts that stopped one household from noticing it.
findings.problem: Inverts the direction of the list. As above, the 'of money' repetitions expand from house to street to city to country, so Kaminsky's catalogue widens to national scale rather than narrowing to 'domestic comforts' (Library of Congress Poetry 180).
findings.correction: while Kaminsky’s repeated “of money” widens from a single house out to a whole “country of money”, indicting a national comfort rather than one household’s.

findings.claim: {"q": "Which phrase is repeated four times to list small domestic comforts?", "a": "'Of money.'"}
findings.problem: The premise is wrong: the four repetitions of 'of money' attach to house, street, city and country — an expanding public scale, not 'small domestic comforts' (Library of Congress Poetry 180; Poetry Out Loud).
findings.correction: {"q": "Which phrase is repeated four times as the poem widens from house to country?", "a": "'Of money.'"}

findings.claim: The phrase '_____' is repeated four times in a list, suggesting small comforts distracted people from the war.
findings.problem: Same misreading of the list's structure: the repetition builds outwards through house, street, city and country of money, so it indicts national wealth, not 'small comforts' (Library of Congress Poetry 180).
findings.correction: The phrase '_____' is repeated four times in a widening list (house, street, city, country), suggesting a whole nation's wealth insulated people from the war.

findings.claim: The poem confesses, 'We lived happily during the war, _____.'
findings.problem: Presents the words in an order that does not occur in the poem. The text reads 'we (forgive us) / lived happily during the war' — the parenthesis interrupts the phrase and appears in the poem's final sentence, not after it (Library of Congress Poetry 180; Poetry Out Loud). Teaching this word order risks students misquoting under closed-book conditions.
findings.correction: The poem's final sentence interrupts itself: 'we (_____) lived happily during the war.'

findings.claim: Both poems use direct address — Douglas to the dead soldier’s photograph, Kaminsky to the reader through “we” — to make guilt personal rather than abstract.
findings.problem: Misdescribes 'Vergissmeinnicht'. In the anthology text the photograph is of the dead soldier's girlfriend — 'the dishonoured picture of his girl / who has put: Steffi. Vergissmeinnicht.' — not a photograph of the soldier. Nor is it addressed: the poem's only imperative, 'Look.', is directed at the speaker's companions/reader. Students repeating this would misidentify a central image.
findings.correction: Both poems pull guilt towards the personal: Douglas points his reader to a specific object — “the dishonoured picture of his girl” found in the gunpit — with the imperative “Look.”, while Kaminsky implicates the reader through the collective “we”.

findings.claim: Compare how Kaminsky in 'We Lived Happily during the War' and Agard in 'Flag' present the idea that ordinary people can be blind to the suffering caused by conflict. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: This question format does not exist on J352/02. Per the stated assessment rules, part a) compares the two poems PRINTED on the paper — the named anthology poem and a thematically linked unseen poem — and part b) asks for detailed exploration of one other anthology poem of the student's choice. There is no question requiring comparison of two anthology poems, so practising this misprepares students for both parts.
findings.correction: The poem printed alongside 'We Lived Happily during the War' is an unseen poem in which a speaker celebrates a national flag while ignoring the cost of the war fought under it. Compare how the two poems present the idea that ordinary people can be blind to the suffering caused by conflict. You should compare the poets' ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]

findings.claim: Mastering: Analyses Agard's imperative 'blind your conscience' against Kaminsky's confessional 'we', showing how both poems expose complicity in different registers.
findings.problem: This marking guidance belongs to the invalid anthology-versus-anthology comparison question above; once that question is reframed as an anthology/unseen comparison (or moved to part b) as a single-poem exploration), the guidance must not reward comparison with a second anthology poem, which part a) never asks for.
findings.correction: Mastering: Sophisticated comparison of complicity and denial, analysing Kaminsky's confessional 'we' and parenthetical 'forgive us' against the unseen poem's tone and structural choices. Secure: Clear comparison of language or structure with relevant quotations from both printed poems. Developing: Some comparison with limited textual support. Emerging: Basic comments on one poem only.

findings.claim: Compare how 'Thirteen' and 'Honour Killing' present identities that are imposed on individuals rather than chosen by them. [type: 20 marks — Anthology and Unseen Comparison]
findings.problem: This invents a task format the paper does not contain. Per the stated assessment rules for J352/02, part a) (20 marks) compares the two poems PRINTED on the paper — the named anthology poem and a thematically linked unseen poem — and part b) (20 marks) asks for detailed exploration of one other anthology poem of the student's choice. There is no anthology-poem-to-anthology-poem comparison question, so practising one under the 'Anthology and Unseen Comparison' tariff misdirects revision.
findings.correction: Replace with a valid part b) task: 'Explore how Dharker presents an identity imposed on the speaker in ‘Honour Killing’.' [type: 20 marks — Single Poem Exploration] — or reframe as part a) with an unseen: 'The poem ‘Thirteen’ and an unseen poem about being defined by others are printed on the exam paper. Compare how the two poets present imposed identity.'

findings.claim: For the second part of the question, choose a comparison poem you can quote from confidently rather than one you only half remember
findings.problem: Misdescribes part b). The stated assessment rules say part b) asks students to explore IN DETAIL one other poem from their anthology, of their own choice; it is not a comparison task. Telling students to treat it as a comparison risks them splitting a 20-mark single-poem answer across two poems.
findings.correction: For the second part of the question you explore one other anthology poem of your own choice in detail — not a comparison — so choose a poem you can quote from confidently rather than one you only half remember; a short, exact phrase used well beats a long, vague paraphrase.

findings.claim: Italicised lines interrupt this future-tense prophecy, marking out the primary school memory as a separate, more innocent voice within the poem.
findings.problem: Unsupported specific claim about the poem's typography. The OCR teacher guide (the only permitted source for this copyright poem) asks only 'Where and why does he use italics in the poem?' and never says what the italics mark; published texts of the poem show the italics falling on the officers' spoken words (e.g. the challenge that the boy fits the description, and the later 'Don't you remember me?'), not on the primary-school memory. Students repeating this in an exam would be inaccurate on a structural point.
findings.correction: Femi also uses italics at points in the poem to set off a separate voice from the future-tense prophecy — look closely at where the italics fall in your copy of the poem and consider whose words they are and why that voice is made to stand out.

findings.claim: a memory from his primary school, when a police officer visited his classroom and smiled at the children, seeming to promise them a bright future
findings.problem: Secondary narrative detail is imprecise: the remembered occasion in the poem is a school assembly at which the officer tells the boy's class they are all supernovas, the biggest and brightest stars; the OCR guide says only that the policeman visited 'the boy's primary' and predicted a bright future. 'Visited his classroom' is not supported.
findings.correction: a memory from his primary school, when the same police officer spoke at a school assembly and told the boy's class they were all bright stars, seeming to promise them a future

findings.claim: Which line in 'Thirteen' alludes to soldiers gambling over a condemned man's body?
findings.problem: In the crucifixion narrative the soldiers cast lots for the condemned man's clothing/belongings, not his body — as the lesson's own content_html correctly states. Femi's shocking move is to transfer the gambling to the boy's organs.
findings.correction: Q: 'Which line in ‘Thirteen’ alludes to soldiers casting lots for a condemned man's belongings?' A: '‘You will watch the two men cast lots for your organs.’'
